reason: Both clear pieces bend light, so they look like the start of the focusing front. The picture also shows the iris controls the opening, but I expect to add it separately.
expectation: The cornea and lens will form a light-focusing front.

effect: The cornea and lens now focus light toward the back; the iris still needs to control the opening.
reaction: The rays meeting at the back make their combined job clearer.
reason: The iris picture shows an opening that narrows, so it belongs with the focusing front to control incoming light.
expectation: The eye front will focus light and control how much enters.

effect: The eye front is complete: the iris controls light entry while the cornea and lens focus it.
reaction: The cutaway makes the separate jobs clear.
reason: The light-sensitive cells and nerve cells match the goal of making a lining that sends signals onward.
expectation: They will form a light-sensitive lining connected to outgoing nerve fibres.

effect: The retina and optic nerve now provide the light-sensitive lining and outgoing signal route.
reaction: The picture makes the new terms easier to connect to their jobs.
reason: The focusing front needs the light-sensitive lining behind it to make an eye.
expectation: The front and retina will join into an eye that can focus light onto the lining.

effect: The focusing front and retina now form an eye with an outgoing optic nerve; it still needs to connect to the body.
reaction: The cutaway shows how the parts fit together.
reason: The goal calls for connecting the eye to the brain, so the eye belongs with the repaired body.
expectation: The eye and its optic nerve will connect to the body's brain.

effect: The eyes are connected to the brain by nerves; the sunlit leaf remains to be seen.
reaction: The nerve route in the cutaway makes the connection clear.
reason: The leaf reflects light, and the connected eyes can now receive it.
expectation: Light reflected from the leaf will enter the eyes and lead to a sight.

effect: The leaf's reflected light reaches the retina, and nerve signals continue to the brain. The sight goal is complete.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the separate pieces connect into a route from leaf to brain.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making the retina and optic nerve was most worthwhile: the picture connected two new names to the light-sensitive lining and its outgoing signal route.

leastWorthwhile.text: Joining the completed eye to the body felt fairly predictable, though it was needed to show the nerve route to the brain.

surprise.text: I was interested that the iris controls how much light enters, while the cornea and lens do the focusing; they have different jobs.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt particularly arbitrary. The pictures and goals made the pairings understandable, although the chapter did not explain in detail how light becomes a nerve signal.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: building the eye and then tracing light to the brain made me curious about how other senses work, even though most combinations were straightforward.
